newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa telecoms bill sets framework for overhaul. [CORRECTED 16:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: S.Africa telecoms bill sets framework for overhaul. [CORRECTED 16:50 GMT]

text.p: South Africa unveiled a long-awaited telecommunications bill on Thursday, setting the regulatory framework for restructuring the industry, including partial privatisation of state-owned utility Telkom.
Minister of Posts and Telecommunications Jay Naidoo said the legislation would be considered by parliament when it reconvened on October 7 and should be passed into law by the year-end.
It sets ground rules for a liberalised telecoms market to be monitored by two independent watchdogs, the South African Telecommunications Regulatory Authority and the Universal Service Agency.
These bodies will ensure fair competition and equitable countrywide coverage, as well as regulating prices via a formula linked to consumer price inflation.

Naidoo reiterated the aim was to conclude a deal by next March or April for a strategic equity partner to take a stake of up to 30 percent in Telkom, in a move seen as spearheading the government's privatisation drive.
Eight potential partners have been identified, but the list may be narrowed in coming weeks.
"We expect that due diligence will begin some time in October and we will be in a position to ask for proposals from possible partners by November," Naidoo said.
"These will then be evaluated and by early February we should have final proposals from shortlisted candidates."

The potential partners are France Telecom, Deutsche Telkom, British Telecommunications Plc, Stet Spa, a Dutch and Swedish consortium of KPN and Telia, Bell Atlantic Corp, South Western Bell Corp and Telekom Malaysia Bhd.
One key issue affecting any bid will be the period of exclusivity granted to Telkom's fixed voice telephony business.
Naidoo argues protection from direct competition is needed to help build universal service and rebalance tariffs.
This period is not spelled out in the bill and will be laid down when Telkom receives a licence next year.
The government wants five to seven (corrects from three to five) years exclusivity, but this is subject to discussion within the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
The WTO has set a deadline of February 27, 1997, for submissions for liberalising telecoms markets.
"We don't think we will have any difficulties at the WTO negotiations. There are countries going for much longer periods of exclusivity than we are," Naidoo said.

The South African government has undertaken to double the number of domestic telephones over the next five years from four million serving mainly white areas at present to eight million, with a much greater penetration in traditionally black areas.
To do this it requires an injection of cash and skills, plus a period of transition from monopoly to free market, Naidoo said.
Nonetheless, the government was committed to opening up the market and the new bill would put South Africa on a par with telecommunications regimes in Argentina, Canada and Britain.
The Telkom deal is South Africa's first major privatisation project and seen as a litmus test of the government's commitment to sell off state assets.

Other states enterprises in line for full or partial privatisation include South African Airways, the airports company, sections of the rail and road transport network, state-owned leisure facilities and, possibly, electricity generator Eskom.
